bibliography.abstract: Visual Place Recognition (VPR) aims to recognize the location of a query image by comparing it with a set of geo-referenced images. Although many datasets have been proposed for VPR, collecting dense and diverse visual data from pedestrian-level viewpoints is still an important need. In this paper, we introduce YILDIZ-VPR, a visual geo-localization dataset collected through repeated walking traversals on the Davutpasa campus of Yildiz Technical University. The dataset includes outdoor scenes captured at different times of day, seasons, and weather conditions. It contains a wide range of visual content, including historical buildings, modern structures, roads, green areas, and wooded regions. Each video was recorded with a GoPro 9 camera and synchronized with GPS sensor data to provide location labels for the extracted frames. In addition to GPS coordinates, the dataset also includes auxiliary sensor information such as gyroscope, speed, and temperature data. With its dense coverage and long-term visual variability, YILDIZ-VPR provides a useful resource for studying image-based and temporal visual place recognition under realistic outdoor conditions.
bibliography.title: YILDIZ-VPR: A Novel Dataset with Dense Coverage Under Diverse Environmental Conditions for Visual Place Recognition

topics.label: Advanced Image and Video Retrieval Techniques

en.caveats: The dataset is restricted to a single university campus, which may limit its representativeness for broader urban or highly structured metropolitan environments.
en.what: The researchers created YILDIZ-VPR, a visual geo-localization dataset collected via repeated walking traversals of the Yildiz Technical University Davutpasa campus using a GoPro 9 camera. The dataset features dense, pedestrian-level outdoor video frames synchronized with GPS coordinates, gyroscope, speed, and temperature data across different times of day, seasons, and weather conditions.
en.why: It provides a dense, multi-sensor pedestrian dataset that captures long-term environmental and seasonal variations, enabling more robust testing of image-based and temporal visual place recognition algorithms in realistic campus environments.
